KEY MESSAGE 1: A deepening trough will result in a 
strengthening coastal low providing a shot of rain on Thursday 
with the potential for a transition to snow in the northeastern 
zones Thursday night.

Complex surface pattern seen this evening across the
Commonwealth of PA with denser, albeit shallow cooler air 
oozing into Northern PA via a light NE wind. Recent analysis at
02Z shows the slow moving cfront located about 30 NM south of 
interstate 80. The boundary separates temps in the mid-upper 40s
to the north from readings in the low to mid 50 across the 
southern half of the state. The primary boundary in the 925-850 
mb layer was located over Northern PA and Southern NY 
respectively. 

As the southerly flow in the 925-850 layer increases by 10-15
kts (enhancing the lift up and over the aforementioned frontal 
boundaries at 952-850 mb) and increasing diff PVA arrives from 
the west over the next several hours, we'll see the precip 
pattern blossom across much of the northern half of CWA. the
bulk of the southern third to half of the CWA will stay mostly 
cloud but dry through daybreak Thu.

Previous Disc...  

The main game in town across central Pennsylvania over the next
week will be the potential for the first accumulating snowfall 
mainly for the higher elevations of central Pennsylvania. As a 
low pressure system approaches the region from the Ohio Valley, 
potential for scattered showers increase this evening into 
tonight. Signals continue for the developing surface low 
pressure to be sub-1000mb as it moves just south of the region 
on Thursday. All guidance points towards increasing moisture 
with southeasterly flow from the Chesapeake Bay into the 
Susquehanna Valley, which will promote more widespread shower 
activity. Current thinking is that there will continue to be 
some orographic enhancement with recent REFS ensemble guidance 
outlining two six-hour blocks (between 12Z Thursday and 00Z 
Friday) with low-end probabilities of exceeding one inch of QPF 
across the Middle Susquehanna Valley where more forcing and 
orographic lift will be in place compared to the Lower 
Susquehanna Valley. Not entirely sold on there being over an 
inch in any six-hour block; however, this signal does outline 
the heavy rain potential. No flooding concerns will exist with 
well-below average precipitation across the entire area over the
last two months. 

Model guidance has also stayed consistent with respect to cold
air wrapping around the back side of this system. The mentions
of frontogenetic forcing, which will bring about lingering
showers across the northeastern zones mentioned in the previous
forecast cycle remains fairly consistent. Current forecast has a
slight uptick in snowfall across our northeastern zones
(Potter/Tioga/Sullivan), where recent REFS total snowfall
probabilities have a greater than 60% chance for receiving
accumulations over one inch. Some isolated instances of
accumulations reaching into the 2-3" range across the higher
elevations of Sullivan County have been outlined in the previous
two forecast cycles, but there's still questions on how long
precipitation lingers across the region. 

------------------------------------------------------------------

KEY MESSAGE 2: Northwesterly flow brings much cooler 
temperatures this weekend, with lake-enhanced snow showers 
continuing Friday into Saturday night.

Cooler temperatures and breezy northwesterly winds will take 
hold of the region as the area of low pressure shifts east 
towards the New England Coast. Wind gusts in the 25-35 mph range
are likely from Thursday night through the weekend. By sunrise 
on Friday, the stratiform precip will be pulling away and north-
south oriented lake effect streamer bands will likely be in its
wake. Typically streamer bands will trend towards a more 
cellular mode with daytime heating. At this time, snowfall 
appears to be the dominant precipitation type across the 
northern/western halves of Pennsylvania with rain prevailing 
elsewhere. That being said cannot completely rule out a 
rain/snow mix further south/east if precipitation rates trend 
higher. The lake effect and upslope snow on the back side of 
this system is expected to produce a coating to one inch of snow
across the Laurels and the northwest mountains with localized 
amounts pushing closer to two inches in the highest elevations.

Chances for precipitation begin to decrease Saturday night into 
Sunday as a subsidence inversion builds in with approaching high
pressure. A slight warming trend emerges into the beginning of 
next week, with temperatures trending closer to climatological 
averages by Tuesday.
